title: STAT 109: Introductory Biostatistics
text:
Welcome to STAT 109: Introductory Biostatistics!
This website contains Rosanna Overholser’s materials for an asynchronous version of STAT 109: Introductory Biostatistics at Cal Poly Humboldt. An asynchronous course means you work through the materials on your own schedule, with support from an expert and your peers along the way. My goal for you isn’t just to finish assignments. By the end of the course, you will have a portfolio of five projects and tworeference sheets that you can continue to use, build on, and share for years to come. And perhaps a few fellow Lumberjacks to meet up with when we all return to campus in the fall.

title: STAT 109: Introductory Biostatistics
text:
Where you are
Most of what you read and work through lives on this website: lectures, labs and project instructions. Canvas is where you submit work, take quizzes, see grades, get feedback, and chat with classmates. The course path lays out a recommended order through the the material in five weeks; the syllabus has the official policies and grading information for the course.

title: STAT 109: Introductory Biostatistics
text:
What you’ll learn
In this class you’ll learn statistical ideas that people use to make decisions and test claims with data. You’ll learn the concepts, but you’ll also learn by doing—carrying out analyses with technology.
When you’re working with a real dataset, point-and-click tools only get you so far. Data usually needs wrangling and cleaning before you can run a test or fit a model. Programming lets you do that work efficiently and leaves a record of what you did. That record matters for reproducible research: someone else (including future you) can follow what happened to the data from start to finish. That’s a big part of why we use code instead of only clicking through menus.
We’ll use R, which is free and widely used by statisticians and researchers who work with messy data. Python is another popular option; its data-processing syntax is similar enough to R’s that you’ll be able to pick it up quickly if you need to later.
We run R in Google Colab notebooks, which are a common way to run Jupyter notebooks with no local installation needed.

title: STAT 109: Introductory Biostatistics
text:
What you’ll build
By the end of the course you’ll have created two reference guides: one for statistical concepts (definitions, notation, methods you want to keep organized) and one for the R programming language (functions, code patterns, notes from your notebooks).
You’ll also complete five projects: applied analyses with write-ups and code. You’ll update the reference sheets a little every module; each project module adds one new project to your portfolio. For three of the projects, you’ll chose a research question that you are interested and then apply methods from class to answer it. For the four, you’ll answer a classmate’s question and for the fifth, you’ll compete with your classmates to make the most accurate set of predictions.
My hope is that you’ll use include these five projects in your portfolio to demonstrate your understanding of the material and your ability to apply it to solve problems that people care about.

section: Why is the course like this?
text:
Why is the course like this?
In 2022, Cal Poly Humboldt became California’s third polytechnic university. Being a polytechnic means emphasizing learning by doing: developing knowledge and skills through hands-on projects connected to the places where we live, work, and play.
This course follows that philosophy. Rather than focusing primarily on watching lectures and taking exams in artificial circumstances, you will learn statistics by conducting investigations, analyzing data, building statistical models, and evaluating evidence. By the end of the course, you will have practiced the same kinds of activities that professionals in business, education, healthcare, government, and community organizations use to answer questions and make decisions.
At the same time, we continue Humboldt’s tradition of place-based learning by connecting with one another and the communities and environments that shape our lives through informal discussions and the course projects.
Cal Poly Humboldt’s motto, Light and Truth, reminds us that education is a search for understanding. Statistics is one of the tools we use in that search. By collecting evidence, asking thoughtful questions, and carefully evaluating uncertainty, we can develop a clearer understanding of the world around us.
This course also reflects values that are central to Cal Poly Humboldt: caring for the environment and for our community. Whether we are studying forests, wildlife, public health, or everyday decisions, statistics helps us learn from evidence and contribute thoughtfully to the well-being of people and the planet.
Finally, this course is built around a particular vision of teaching and learning. Rather than viewing the professor as a “sage on the stage” whose job is to deliver answers, I see learning as a shared journey of inquiry. Together we will ask questions, gather evidence, build models, test ideas, and learn from mistakes. Along the way, you will have access to many resources, including your classmates, course materials, modern computational tools, AI assistants, and me. The goal is not simply to find answers, but to develop the habits of mind needed to ask good questions, think critically about evidence, work effectively with others, and solve challenging problems. My role is not only to teach statistics, but also to guide and support you as you build those skills.

title: Lab 2 Demo: Random grid sites
text:
NoteOpen in Google Colab (R)




Open demo in Colab
Open student exercise in Colab

After a notebook opens, use Runtime → Change runtime type and select R if needed.


Goal: Start Lab 2 with a probability question on an equally likely sample space, then show how to compute it by counting and by simulation in R.


Before the 2D grid, we practice the same ideas on a 1D line of 5 sites.
We label sites as:
\[
S = \{1,2,3,4,5\}
\]
We choose 2 distinct sites without replacement, so the equally likely sample space is all 2-site sets:
\[
|S_2| = \binom{5}{2} = 10
\]


The “end sites” are 1 and 5.
Use the complement (“no ends” means both picks are from {2,3,4}):
\[
P(\text{at least one end})
= 1 - \frac{\binom{3}{2}}{\binom{5}{2}}
= 1 - \frac{3}{10}
= \frac{7}{10}
\]



Adjacent pairs are:

{1,2}, {2,3}, {3,4}, {4,5} (4 pairs total)

So:
\[
P(\text{adjacent}) = \frac{4}{\binom{5}{2}} = \frac{4}{10} = 0.4
\]



set.seed(109)

sites <- 1:5
B <- 10000

at_least_one_end <- logical(B)
adjacent <- logical(B)

for (b in 1:B) {
  draws <- sample(sites, size = 2, replace = FALSE)
  a <- draws[1]
  c <- draws[2]

  # "at least one end" using the Lab 1 sum idea
  at_least_one_end[b] <- sum(c(a == 1, a == 5, c == 1, c == 5)) > 0

  # adjacent on a line if they differ by 1
  adjacent[b] <- (abs(a - c) == 1)
}

mean(at_least_one_end)
mean(adjacent)





We have an \(N \times N\) grid of possible sampling sites. Each site is equally likely.
For this demo, we will keep things realistic and simple:

We select 2 distinct sites without replacement from the grid.
Every unordered pair of sites is equally likely.

So the sample space size is:
\[
|S| = \binom{N^2}{2}
\]

Total sites: \(N^2\)
Corner sites: \(4\)
Edge sites (including corners): \(4N - 4\)

Define:

\(p_\text{corner} = \frac{4}{N^2}\)
\(p_\text{edge} = \frac{4N-4}{N^2}\)






Types

numeric vs integer vs character vs logical
class(x) (and optionally typeof(x))

Vectors

c(...) to create vectors
length(x) to check size
bracketing x[i] and bracketing with a logical vector x[x > 5]
element-by-element operations: x + 1, x * 2, x == y

Matrices

matrix(...) to create a matrix
dim(m) to check size
bracketing m[row, col], extracting rows/cols with m[1, ], m[, 2]

Simulation + loops

sample(..., replace = FALSE) (choose distinct sites)
%in% for “is it in this set?”
placeholders: logical(B), numeric(B)
for (b in 1:B) { ... } storing one result per run
probability by simulation: mean(TRUE/FALSE)




# Types
x_num <- 3.5
x_int <- 3L
x_chr <- "site"
x_log <- (3 < 5)

class(x_num); class(x_int); class(x_chr); class(x_log)

# Vector + length + scalar operations
v <- c(2, 4, 6, 8, 10)
length(v)
v + 1
v * 2

# Matrix + dim + bracketing
m <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3)
dim(m)
m[2, 2]
m[1, ]
m[, 2]





We are choosing 2 distinct sites from \(N^2\) equally likely sites.
There are 4 corners and \(N^2 - 4\) non-corners.
Use the complement (“no corners”):
\[
P(\text{at least one corner})
= 1 - P(\text{no corners})
= 1 - \frac{\binom{N^2 - 4}{2}}{\binom{N^2}{2}}
\]




Edges (including corners) total \(4N - 4\) sites, so non-edges total:
\[
N^2 - (4N - 4) = (N-2)^2
\]
Use the complement (“no edges”):
\[
P(\text{at least one edge})
= 1 - P(\text{no edges})
= 1 - \frac{\binom{(N-2)^2}{2}}{\binom{N^2}{2}}
\]




We will say two sites are adjacent if they are 4-neighbors (up/down/left/right).


In an \(N\times N\) grid:

Horizontal adjacent pairs: \(N(N-1)\)
Vertical adjacent pairs: \(N(N-1)\)

So total adjacent (unordered) pairs:
\[
2N(N-1)
\]
Total possible unordered pairs of sites:
\[
\binom{N^2}{2}
\]
Therefore:
\[
P(\text{adjacent}) = \frac{2N(N-1)}{\binom{N^2}{2}}
\]





Pick values that are easy to talk through in class. For example:

\(N = 5\) (a \(5\times 5\) grid, 25 sites)

Then:

Total pairs: \(\binom{25}{2} = 300\)
Adjacent pairs: \(2N(N-1)=2\cdot 5\cdot 4=40\)

We can compute the three probabilities in R.
N <- 5
total_pairs <- choose(N^2, 2)

# 1) at least one corner
p_at_least_one_corner <- 1 - choose(N^2 - 4, 2) / total_pairs

# 2) at least one edge
p_at_least_one_edge <- 1 - choose((N - 2)^2, 2) / total_pairs

# 3) adjacent
p_adjacent <- (2 * N * (N - 1)) / total_pairs

p_at_least_one_corner
p_at_least_one_edge
p_adjacent




We simulate \(B\) random samples of 2 distinct sites, and estimate probabilities by proportions (mean(TRUE/FALSE)).
We label each grid cell with a string "i,j" so the sampled sites look like coordinates you’d write by hand.
New-to-Lab-1/2 note: this uses paste() to create "i,j" labels and strsplit() + as.numeric() to turn "i,j" back into numbers for the adjacency check.
set.seed(109)

N <- 5
B <- 10000

# Make a grid whose entries look like "i,j" (row,col)
grid <- matrix("", nrow = N, ncol = N)
for (i in 1:N) {
  for (j in 1:N) {
    grid[i, j] <- paste(i, j, sep = ",")
  }
}

corners <- c(grid[1,1], grid[1,N], grid[N,1], grid[N,N])
edges   <- c(grid[1, ], grid[N, ], grid[2:(N-1), 1], grid[2:(N-1), N])

at_least_one_corner <- logical(B)
at_least_one_edge   <- logical(B)
adjacent            <- logical(B)

for (b in 1:B) {
  picks <- sample(grid, size = 2, replace = FALSE)
  s1 <- picks[1]
  s2 <- picks[2]

  rc1 <- as.numeric(strsplit(s1, ",")[[1]])
  rc2 <- as.numeric(strsplit(s2, ",")[[1]])

  r1 <- rc1[1]; c1 <- rc1[2]
  r2 <- rc2[1]; c2 <- rc2[2]

  # keep the Lab 1 "sum of TRUE/FALSE" idea (avoid new | and & operators)
  at_least_one_corner[b] <- sum(c(s1 %in% corners, s2 %in% corners)) > 0
  at_least_one_edge[b]   <- sum(c(s1 %in% edges,   s2 %in% edges))   > 0

  same_row_adj <- (r1 == r2) * (abs(c1 - c2) == 1)
  same_col_adj <- (c1 == c2) * (abs(r1 - r2) == 1)
  adjacent[b] <- sum(c(same_row_adj, same_col_adj)) > 0
}

mean(at_least_one_corner)
mean(at_least_one_edge)
mean(adjacent)





Equally likely sample space: every 2-site sample (without replacement) is equally likely.
Counting: corners = 4; edges = \(4N-4\); total sites = \(N^2\); total pairs = \(\binom{N^2}{2}\).
Matrices + bracketing: grid <- matrix("", ...), corners <- c(grid[1,1], ...), etc.
For loop: pre-allocate storage (logical(B)) and store one result per iteration.
Probability by simulation: mean(TRUE/FALSE) gives a proportion.

title: Lab 7
text:
Quick guide: 95% interval choices + conditions

A) One mean, population effectively infinite (no FPC)
Use a t-interval:
\[
\bar{x} \pm t^{*}_{df=n-1}\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
Conditions (typical intro stat version):
- SRS (or random sample), independent observations
- Data are roughly symmetric (normal) or n is moderately large (greater than 30)



B) One mean, finite population (use FPC)
Use a t-interval with finite population correction (SRS without replacement from a known finite list):
\[
\bar{x} \pm t^{*}_{df=n-1}\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\sqrt{\frac{N-n}{N-1}}
\]
Conditions:
- SRS without replacement from a finite population of known size N
- Data are roughly symmetric (normal) or n is moderately large (greater than 30)



C) One proportion, population effectively infinite (no FPC), large-sample “normal” CI
\[
\hat{p} \pm z^{*} \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}
\]
Conditions: - SRS (or random sample), independent - Large counts: \(n\hat{p} \ge 10\) and \(n(1-\hat{p})\ge 10\)



D) One proportion, finite population (use FPC), large-sample “normal” CI
\[
\hat{p} \pm z^{*} \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}} \sqrt{\frac{N-n}{N-1}}
\]
Conditions: - SRS without replacement from a finite population of known size N - Large counts: \(n\hat{p} \ge 10\) and \(n(1-\hat{p})\ge 10\)



E) One proportion, small sample (or rare event): exact binomial CI
If \(n\hat{p} < 10\) or \(n(1-\hat{p}) < 10\), prefer an exact binomial CI (Clopper–Pearson): - In R: binom.test(x, n) then .$conf.int Conditions: - Fixed n, independent binary trials with common success probability (binomial model) - (If sampling without replacement from a finite population and n/N is small, binomial is a reasonable approximation.)

title: Lab 7
section: Problem 1 — One mean, population effectively infinite (no FPC)
text:
Problem 1 — One mean, population effectively infinite (no FPC)
A college instructor wants to estimate the mean number of minutes per day that students in an intro stats course spend on the course website. A random sample of n = 25 students was taken, and their times (minutes) were collected.
Tasks (student version): - Decide which interval formula to use
- Compute the sample mean and SD
- Make a histogram with stacked dots (like in the sample project)
- Compute a 95% CI for the mean

Desired output (what your code should produce)

A printed sample mean and SD

A plot (histogram + dots)

A printed 95% CI for the mean (two endpoints)



Code
x <- c(12, 18, 25, 9, 31, 16, 20, 22, 14, 3, 19, 11, 24, 30, 15, 15, 21, 26, 13, 28, 10, 23, 29, 18, 33)

mean(x)


[1] 19.4


Code
sd(x)


[1] 7.72442


Code
ggplot(data.frame(x=x), aes(x=x)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, boundary = 0) +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth = 1, stackdir = "up", dotsize = 0.75) +
  labs(title="Daily minutes on course website (sample)",
       x="Minutes per day", y="Count")









Code
# 95% t-interval (no FPC)
mean(x) + c(-1,1)*qt(0.975, df=length(x)-1) * (sd(x)/sqrt(length(x)))


[1] 16.21152 22.58848


Code
# no math equation method
t.test(x)

section: Problem 2 — One mean, finite population (use FPC)
text:
Problem 2 — One mean, finite population (use FPC)
A school district has a list of N = 300 high school classrooms. They want to estimate the mean number of chairs per classroom. A simple random sample (without replacement) of n = 30 classrooms was selected. The chair counts were counted.
Tasks (student version): - Decide which interval formula to use
- Compute mean and SD
- Make a histogram with stacked dots
- Compute a 95% CI for the mean with FPC


Code
N <- 300
x <- c(28, 30, 32, 27, 27, 33, 33, 26, 30, 30, 28, 29, 35, 27, 32, 32, 28, 30, 29, 33, 26, 34, 28, 31, 30, 27, 32, 29, 33, 28)

mean(x)


[1] 29.9


Code
sd(x)


[1] 2.523681


Code

  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, boundary = 0) +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth = 1, stackdir="up", dotsize=0.5) +
  labs(title="Chairs per classroom (SRS from finite population)",

title: Lab 7
section: Extra (optional): confidence intervals with the survey package
text:
Extra (optional): confidence intervals with the survey package
Pick either the mean subsection or the proportion subsection below—each is self-contained.


One mean (Problems 1–2)
Idea: For a numeric outcome, svymean(~measurement, design) estimates the population mean. confint(...) gives a 95% interval with a t-style SE when the design is a simple random sample (same spirit as t.test).
Steps (minimal):

Build a data.frame with one row per sampled unit and a column for the numeric measurement (e.g. minutes, chair count).
Call svydesign(ids = ~1, data = ...) — ids = ~1 means “no clusters; each row is its own primary unit.”
Finite population (Problem 2): add a column equal to N (total population size) on every row and set fpc = ~N in svydesign. Infinite population (Problem 1): omit fpc.
confint(svymean(~measurement, design)) — interval for the population mean.

This matches Problems 1–2 with less algebra in R.


Code
library(survey)

# --- Problem 1 style (no FPC): same x as above ---
x <- c(12, 18, 25, 9, 31, 16, 20, 22, 14, 3, 19, 11, 24, 30, 15, 15, 21, 26, 13, 28, 10, 23, 29, 18, 33)
d1 <- data.frame(x = x)
w1 <- svydesign(ids = ~1, data = d1)
confint(svymean(~x, w1))   # matches the usual one-sample t interval


     2.5 %   97.5 %
x 16.37208 22.42792


Code
# --- Problem 2 style (FPC): N = 300 classrooms, same x as above ---
N <- 300
x2 <- c(28, 30, 32, 27, 27, 33, 33, 26, 30, 30, 28, 29, 35, 27, 32, 32, 28, 30, 29, 33, 26, 34, 28, 31, 30, 27, 32, 29, 33, 28)
d2 <- data.frame(x = x2, N = N)
w2 <- svydesign(ids = ~1, data = d2, fpc = ~N)
confint(svymean(~x, w2))


     2.5 %   97.5 %
x 29.04327 30.75673





One proportion (Problems 3–4)
Idea: For a Yes/No (or 0/1) outcome, svymean(~outcome, design) gives \(\hat{p}\). confint(...) uses a large-sample normal approximation for the proportion (same spirit as the Wald formulas in the quick guide).
Steps (minimal):

Build a data.frame with one row per sampled unit and a column for the Yes/No (or 0/1) outcome.
Call svydesign(ids = ~1, data = ...) — ids = ~1 means “no clusters; each row is its own primary unit.”
Finite population (Problem 4): add a column equal to N (total population size) on every row and set fpc = ~N in svydesign. Infinite population (Problem 3): omit fpc.
confint(svymean(~outcome, design)) — interval for the population proportion.

This matches Problems 3–4 with less algebra in R.


Code
library(survey)

# --- Problem 3 style (no FPC): n = 220, x = 80 with part-time job ---
job <- c(rep(TRUE, 80), rep(FALSE, 220 - 80))
d3  <- data.frame(job = job)
w3  <- svydesign(ids = ~1, data = d3)
confint(svymean(~job, w3))


             2.5 %    97.5 %
jobFALSE 0.5726529 0.7000743
jobTRUE  0.2999257 0.4273471


Code
# --- Problem 4 style (FPC): N = 1500, n = 108, x = 20 “>50 years” ---
d4 <- data.frame(
  old50 = c(rep(TRUE, 20), rep(FALSE, 108 - 20)),
  N     = 1500
)
w4 <- svydesign(ids = ~1, data = d4, fpc = ~N)
confint(svymean(~old50, w4))


               2.5 %    97.5 %
old50FALSE 0.7439121 0.8857175
old50TRUE  0.1142825 0.2560879

title: Module 1 — Read 0
text:
Big question: Is what we observed surprising?
Project: Project 1 — Testing a Claim · Sample report: ESP binomial test (PDF) · Next: Read 1






NoteShort read — start here



This page is a five-minute orientation, not the textbook. Read it once before Read 1 so you know where Module 1 is heading.




Imagine you watch a repeatable process many times. You count how often something “succeeds.” After \(n = 25\) trials you have \(x\) successes and an observed proportion \(\hat{p} = x/n\).
That number lives in the world we observe — real data from your study.
Before you can say whether \(x\) is unusual, you enter the world we imagine. You pick a value for \(p\) (probability of success on one trial) and pretend that value is true. That assumption defines a binomial model: if \(H_0\) were correct, what counts would be typical?
The p-value answers: If my imagined model were true, how often would I see something at least this extreme? A small p-value means your observed \(x\) would be rare under that model — the data and the claim in \(H_0\) do not fit well.
You will not need every formula on this page yet. The point is to see the arc of Project 1 before the readings and labs fill in the vocabulary.



Open the sample one-page write-up — ESP binomial test (PDF). It is a finished Project 1 report for an ESP study. Do not copy ESP as your topic — it is a class example. Use the PDF to see shape and tone, not your research question.
Read the sample with these questions in mind:



Section
What to notice
Why it matters for your project




Introduction
Research question, motivation, parameter \(p\), \(H_0\) and \(H_a\) with a numeric null
You will state these before collecting \(n=25\) trials (milestone hub · notebook)


Data collection
How, when, where — enough detail to repeat the study
Your process must satisfy all four BRP conditions (binary, independent, fixed \(p\), fixed \(n\))


Descriptive statistics
\(x\), \(n\), \(\hat{p}\), and a simple chart
Describes the world you observed


Inferential statistics
Bar plot of the null binomial model (dbinom + geom_col), vertical line at your \(x\), p-value from pbinom
Shows the world you imagine and how surprising your data is


Conclusion
One clear sentence tying p-value to the research question
Not “accept/reject \(H_0\)” — interpret evidence in context









ImportantOne mistake to avoid early



The p-value is not the probability that \(H_0\) is true. It is the probability of data at least this extreme, assuming \(H_0\) is true. You will say more about this in Read 2; keep the distinction in mind when you read the sample conclusion.





By the end of Module 1 you will:

Choose your own binomial process (\(n = 25\)), not ESP or other course examples.
Defend the four BRP conditions for your context.
Collect data, build the null model in R, compute a p-value, and write a one-page report with the same section headings as the sample.

The sample shows the deliverable. Read 1 and Read 2 teach the ideas; the demo lab and exercise lab teach the code; the Project 1 page has the full rubric and milestone checklist.




Skim the sample PDF once (5–10 minutes).
Open Project 1 and note the due dates on the course path.
Start Read 1 — probability language through the binomial pmf.

When you finish Read 1, take Quiz A (Def & Notation), then continue with Read 2.

title: Module 1 — Read 1
text:
Project: Project 1 — Testing a Claim · Preview: Read 0 (sample tour) · Next on the course path: Quiz A (Def & Notation), then Read 2.
If you have not skimmed the sample ESP report yet, start with Read 0 (~5 minutes). This reading is your self-paced textbook for Module 1, Part 1. Work one section at a time; answer the Check yourself boxes before moving on (same ideas appear on Quiz A).


Work through all seven sections below in order. Each section has Check yourself boxes before you move on.
After this reading you should be able to:


Probability as data vs theory

Compute counts, proportions, and percentages for an event across repeated trials.
Use symbols \(x\), \(n\), \(\hat{p}\), and \(P(\text{event})\) for data vs theoretical probability.
Distinguish observed outcomes from theoretical probability in a random process.
State three rules that probabilities must satisfy.
Define probability and connect it to long-run relative frequency.




Probability calculations the long way — sample spaces and events

Define and identify sample space, outcome, and event for a trial.
Use notation \(P(A)\) for the probability of an event.
State and use the formula for \(P(A)\) when outcomes in the sample space are equally likely.




Addition rule for probability

State the addition rule for any two events \(A\) and \(B\).
Use the addition rule to compute \(P(A \text{ or } B)\), including overlapping events.
Apply special cases: complement rule and non-overlapping events.




Conditional probability and multiplication rule

State the definition of conditional probability and compute \(P(A \mid B)\).
Use the multiplication rule to compute \(P(A \text{ and } B)\).
Decide whether two events are independent using equivalent criteria.




Permutations and combinations

Distinguish settings where order matters (permutations) from where it does not (combinations).
Use \(_nP_r\) and \(_nC_r\) (or \(\binom{n}{r}\)) to solve counting problems.
Relate factorials to the permutation and combination formulas.




From coin tosses to the binomial random process

Define a discrete random variable and its probability distribution (pdf).
Define a binomial random variable and a binomial random process.
Match notation (\(n\), \(x\), \(p\)) and the four conditions for a binomial process to a coin-toss setting.
Express \(P(X = x)\) using the binomial pdf.




Practice — binomial random process

Decide whether a scenario satisfies the four binomial conditions and justify your answer.
Identify \(n\), \(p\), and the random variable \(X\) for a binomial count.
Write and evaluate probabilities using the binomial pdf; use mean \(\mu = np\) and SD \(\sigma = \sqrt{np(1-p)}\) as needed.






Learning Outcomes:
By the end of today’s lecture, you should be able to:

Compute counts, proportions, and percentages of a particular event occurring in a number of trials.
Use symbols \((x, n, \hat{p}, P(\text{event}))\) correctly to describe observed data and theoretical probability.
Distinguish between observed outcomes (data) and theoretical probability.
Describe three rules that probabilities must satisfy.
State the definition of probability and connect it to the idea of long-run relative frequency in a repeatable random process.











NoteExample in-class data (illustrative)



Suppose three students record: Rosanna 7 heads in 10 tosses (\(\hat{p}=0.7\)); You 4 heads in 10 (\(\hat{p}=0.4\)); Neighbor 6 heads in 12 (\(\hat{p}=0.5\)). Counts and proportions differ because \(n\) and randomness differ.


Let’s toss a coin a few times in class, keeping track of the tosses that land “heads.”



Count of heads (\(x\)): 7
Total tosses (\(n\)): 10
Proportion (\(\hat{p}\)): 0.7
Percentage: 70%





Count of heads (\(x\)): 4
Total tosses (\(n\)): 10
Proportion (\(\hat{p}\)): 0.4
Percentage: 40%





Count of heads (\(x\)): 6
Total tosses (\(n\)): 12
Proportion (\(\hat{p}\)): 0.5
Percentage: 50%

What’s the highest count of heads? 7 (Rosanna)
Most tosses? 12 (neighbor)
Highest proportion of heads? 0.7 (Rosanna)
Highest percentage of heads? 70% (Rosanna)
Comments:
If we care about comparing coins (with the same number of tosses), then \(\hat{p}\) (proportion) is the best summary.
If we care about getting lots of “heads” then \(x\) (count) is the best summary.
The summary of total tosses (\(n\)) tells us how much data we collected / how precise the proportion can be.
Question: Rosanna keeps tossing her coin forever. What would we expect?

Data (what happened): varies from sample to sample (e.g. \(\hat{p}\) bounces around)
Theory (long run): approaches 0.5 for a fair coin






Fill in each definition in your own words:

Sample space:


Outcome:


Event:








ImportantNotation: Data vs theory




We’ll use two colors: one for observed data and another for theoretical quantities.
Async note: In class we color-code theoretical vs observed quantities. On your own, pick two highlighters and use them consistently for \(P(\text{event})\) vs \(\hat{p}\).

\(x\) = count of “successes” in \(n\) observed trials
\(n\) = number of observed trials
\(\hat{p} = x/n\) = observed proportion of successes in our trials
Percentage of observed trials that were a success \(= 100 \cdot \hat{p}\)
\(P(\text{event})\) = probability of an event

The notation for probability, \(P(\text{event})\), is in the same format as notation for functions in high school algebra:

\(=\) reads as “is” (or “equals”)
\(()\) reads as “of” — the event inside the parentheses (not multiplication!)

\(Y = f(x)\) reads as “\(y\) is the value of the function whose name is \(f\) when \(x\) is put in.”
\(Y = P(A)\) reads as “\(y\) is the value of probability when the event under consideration is \(A\).”






Suppose we toss a coin 20 times and see 15 heads.

\(x = 15\)
\(n = 20\)
\(\hat{p} = 15/20 = 0.75\)
Percentage \(= 75\%\)
Theoretical \(P(\text{Heads}) = 0.5\) (for a fair coin)




A coin is tossed 10 times and comes up heads 3 times. Fill in:

\(x = 3\)
\(n = 10\)
\(\hat{p} = 3/10 = 0.3\)
Percentage \(= 30\%\)
Theoretical \(P(\text{Heads}) = 0.5\)




Suppose a fair 6-sided die is rolled 24 times and we see the number “5” exactly 2 times.

\(x = 2\)
\(n = 24\)
\(\hat{p} = 2/24 \approx 0.083\)
Percentage \(\approx 8.3\%\)
Theoretical \(P(\text{"5"}) = 1/6\)




A die is rolled 30 times and shows “1” exactly 10 times. Fill in:

\(x = 10\)
\(n = 30\)
\(\hat{p} = 10/30 \approx 0.333\)
Percentage \(\approx 33.3\%\)
Theoretical \(P(\text{"1"}) = 1/6\)








ImportantRules for probabilities (axioms)



All probabilities must satisfy:

\(0 \le P(A) \le 1\) for any event \(A\)
Total probability across all possible outcomes \(= 1\)
If \(A\) and \(B\) are two events with no overlap, then \(P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B)\)






Coin: \(P(\text{Heads}) + P(\text{Tails}) =\) 1
Die: \(P(\text{"1"}) + P(\text{"2"}) + \cdots + P(\text{"6"}) =\) 1
Die: \(P(\text{"1"}) + P(\text{"2"}) =\) \(1/3\)
\(P(A) = 70\) is invalid (probabilities must be between 0 and 1)
\(-0.5 = P(B)\) is invalid (cannot be negative)
\(P(D) = 0.7\) is valid








ImportantDefinition: Probability



\(P(\text{Event})\) is the proportion of times the event occurs out of the number of trials as the trial is repeated infinitely many times.
Probability is tied to:

A specific random process (repeating a trial with uncertain outcome infinitely many times)
Long-run relative frequency (a.k.a. “proportion”) of an event occurring









TipCheck yourself — Data, notation, and probability




A fair coin is tossed 20 times and shows 9 heads. What are \(x\), \(n\), and \(\hat{p}\)?
In one or two sentences, what is the difference between \(\hat{p}\) and \(P(\text{event})\)?
What is the definition of \(P(\text{Event})\) in terms of long-run relative frequency?
State the three rules (axioms) that all probabilities must satisfy.
Define sample space, outcome, and event.
A coin is tossed 10 times with 3 heads. Compute \(\hat{p}\) and the percentage of heads.





Click to reveal answers


\(x = 9\), \(n = 20\), \(\hat{p} = 9/20 = 0.45\).
\(\hat{p}\) is the observed proportion from data in your sample. \(P(\text{event})\) is the long-run theoretical probability for the random process.
\(P(\text{Event})\) is the proportion of times the event occurs when the trial is repeated infinitely many times.

\(0 \le P(A) \le 1\). (2) \(P(S) = 1\). (3) If \(A\) and \(B\) do not overlap, \(P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B)\).

Sample space \(S\): all possible outcomes of a trial. Outcome: one element of \(S\). Event: a set of one or more outcomes (often written \(A\), \(B\), …).
\(\hat{p} = 3/10 = 0.3\); percentage \(= 30\%\).







Probability calculations the “long way”




Define and identify the following terms for a given trial:

Sample space
Outcome
Event

Use appropriate notation for the probability of an event, \(P(A)\)
State and use the formula for the probability of an event if the outcomes in the sample space are equally likely.





Let’s define the following terms:






ImportantDefinition: Sample space



The sample space \(S\) is the set of all possible outcomes of a trial.


An outcome is one element of the sample space (one possible result of a trial).



An event is a set of one or more outcomes of a trial, usually written with an uppercase letter such as \(A\), \(B\), or \(H\) (for “heads”).







Fill in the meaning or notation for each of the following:
Suppose that a single six-sided die is rolled.






NoteWorked solution — set notation (one die roll)




\(S = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\)
Let \(A\) \(= \{5, 6\}\) (die shows 5 or 6)
Not \(A\) means \(A^c\) — the die shows 1, 2, 3, or 4
\(B = \{2, 4, 6\}\) (even)
\(A\) and \(B\) \(= \{6\}\)
\(A\) or \(B\) \(= \{2, 4, 5, 6\}\)
\(A\) given \(B\): assuming \(B\) occurred, what is the chance \(A\) also occurred?







Translate the following “sentences” to English:

\(P(A) = 0.7\)
\(P(A \text{ and } B) = 0.2\)
\(P(\text{not } A) = 0.1\)
\(P(A|B) = 0.25\)







NoteWorked translations — probability notation




\(P(A)=0.7\): 70% chance event \(A\) occurs.
\(P(A\text{ and }B)=0.2\): 20% chance both \(A\) and \(B\) occur.
\(P(\text{not }A)=0.1\): 10% chance \(A\) does not occur.
\(P(A|B)=0.25\): given \(B\) occurred, there is a 25% chance \(A\) also occurs.







Fill in the blanks:






NoteWorked solution — probability axioms




\(0 \le P(A) \le 1\)
\(P(S) = 1\)
\(P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B)\) when \(A\) and \(B\) do not overlap




Note: “axiom” is a type of rule that we must merely “agree” is true, rather than being able to “prove” that it is true.

Translate the following sentence to correct probability notation:
“The chance of it raining in the next 10 minutes is 80%”
Answer: \(P(\text{rain in next 10 minutes}) = 0.80\)







ImportantRule: Equally likely outcomes



If all outcomes in the sample space \(S\) of a trial are equally likely, then
\[P(A) = \frac{|A|}{|S|}\]
where \(A\) is any event that is contained in \(S\), and the notation \(|\text{set}|\) is the number of outcomes in the set.






Suppose a fair coin is tossed 2 times.

List the sample space \(S\) of this experiment
List the outcomes in the sample space that are in the event \(B =\) “the coin lands heads at least once”
Find \(P(B)\).







NoteWorked solution — two coin tosses




\(S = \{\text{HH, HT, TH, TT}\}\)
\(B = \{\text{HH, HT, TH}\}\) (“heads at least once”)
\(P(B) = 3/4\)







Suppose a fair die is rolled twice.

List the sample space \(S\) of this experiment
List the outcomes in the sample space that are in the event \(C =\) “the sum of the two rolls is 7”
Find \(P(C)\)







NoteWorked solution — two dice (sum is 7)




\(|S| = 36\) ordered pairs.
\(C = \{(1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1)\}\)
\(P(C) = 6/36 = 1/6\)







Suppose Allen, Beth and Cal are in an elevator, each holding a green lunchbox when an earthquake occurs. In the resulting chaos, their lunch boxes are dropped and shuffled around. Assuming they each pick up one lunch box, find the probability that they each pick up their own lunch box.






NoteWorked solution — lunch boxes



There are \(3! = 6\) equally likely assignments. Only 1 gives everyone their own box: \(P = 1/6\).






Suppose a fair coin is tossed three times. Let \(A\) be the event “the coin lands heads at least once”. Find \(P(A)\).






NoteWorked solution — three coin tosses



\(P(\text{at least one head}) = 1 - P(\text{TTT}) = 1 - 1/8 = 7/8\).








TipCheck yourself — Sample spaces and equally likely outcomes




What is \(|S|\) when a fair die is rolled twice and outcomes are listed as ordered pairs?
State the probability rule when all outcomes in \(S\) are equally likely.
Two fair coin tosses: list \(S\) and find \(P(\text{at least one tail})\).
Two dice: how many outcomes give a sum of 11? What is \(P(\text{sum is 11})\)?
Translate \(P(A) = 0.7\) into a complete English sentence.
Three coin tosses: find \(P(\text{at least one head})\).





Click to reveal answers


\(|S| = 36\) (6 choices on the first roll × 6 on the second).
\(P(A) = |A| / |S|\) — the number of outcomes in \(A\) divided by the number in \(S\).
\(S = \{\text{HH, HT, TH, TT}\}\). Event has 3 outcomes; \(P = 3/4\).
Two outcomes: (5,6) and (6,5). \(P = 2/36 = 1/18\).
There is a 70% probability (or 0.7 chance) that event \(A\) occurs.
Complement: no heads has probability \((1/2)^3 = 1/8\). So \(P(\text{at least one H}) = 1 - 1/8 = 7/8\).






Learning Outcomes:

State the Addition Rule for any two events
Use the addition rule to compute the probability of events A or B, being aware of special cases.








ImportantDefinition: Addition rule



For any two events \(A\) and \(B\),
\[P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B)\]
Equivalently, \(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\).


Visualizing the Addition Rule with a Venn Diagram






NoteVenn diagram idea



Draw overlapping circles for \(A\) and \(B\). \(P(A\text{ or }B)\) covers both circles but subtract the overlap \(P(A\text{ and }B)\) so it is not counted twice.


Example: Suppose a class consists of 20 students.  Of these students, 12 have backpacks and 3 have hats.  There is only 1 student with both a backpack and a hat. 
Suppose one student is randomly selected from the 20.  What is the probability this student will either have a backpack OR have a hat?






NoteWorked solution — backpacks and hats (20 students)



\(P(\text{backpack or hat}) = 12/20 + 3/20 - 1/20 = 14/20 = 0.7\).


Practice Problem: Suppose a class consists of 30 students.  Of these students, 8 like to go sky diving and 20 like to go surfing.  There are 7 students that like both sky diving and surfing.
Suppose one student is randomly selected from the 30.  What is the probability this student will like sky diving OR surfing






NoteWorked solution — sky diving or surfing



\(P = 8/30 + 20/30 - 7/30 = 21/30 = 0.7\).



Special Cases of the Addition Rule






ImportantDefinition: Complement rule



For any event \(A\),
\[P(\text{not } A) = P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)\]








ImportantDefinition: Disjoint (non-overlapping) events



If \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint (non-overlapping), then \(P(A \text{ and } B) = 0\) and
\[P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B)\]


Example: Suppose the probability of it snowing at least once this November is 0.83.  what is the probability that it will not snow at all this November?






NoteWorked solution — complement



\(P(\text{no snow}) = 1 - 0.83 = 0.17\).


Example: Suppose that a brand of gummy vitamins come in three animal shapes: Lions, tigers or bears .  The company creates the gummies as follows: 30% of the shapes are bears, 30% are tigers and 40% are lions. 
What is the probability that a randomly selected gummy will be either a bear or a tiger?






NoteWorked solution — disjoint gummies



Bear and tiger are disjoint: \(P = 0.30 + 0.30 = 0.60\).


Practice Problem: Suppose a card is drawn from a standard 52 card deck.  What is the probability the card is…

A “face” card (king, queen or jack)?
An Ace?
Not an Ace?







NoteWorked solution — card from deck




Face cards: \(12/52 = 3/13\). b. Ace: \(4/52 = 1/13\). c. Not an Ace: \(48/52 = 12/13\).









TipCheck yourself — Addition rule




State the addition rule for any events \(A\) and \(B\).
State the complement rule for event \(A\).
If \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint, what is \(P(A \text{ and } B)\)? Write the simplified addition rule.
Class: 40 with backpacks, 10 with hats, 5 with both (out of 65). Find \(P(\text{backpack or hat})\).
If \(P(\text{rains at least once in July}) = 0.91\), find \(P(\text{no rain in July})\).





Click to reveal answers


\(P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B)\).
\(P(A^c) = P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A)\).
\(P(A \text{ and } B) = 0\) and \(P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B)\).
\(P(A)=40/65\), \(P(B)=10/65\), \(P(A\text{ and }B)=5/65\). \(P(A\text{ or }B)=45/65 \approx 0.69\).
\(P(\text{no rain}) = 1 - 0.91 = 0.09\).






Learning Outcomes:

State the definition of conditional probability and compute \(P(A \mid B)\).
Use the multiplication rule to compute \(P(A \text{ and } B)\).
Determine whether two events are independent (using equivalent criteria).








ImportantDefinition: Conditional probability



Notation: \(P(A \mid B)\) means “the probability event \(A\) occurs given event \(B\) occurred.”
Definition: For events \(A\) and \(B\) with \(P(B) > 0\),
\[
P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \text{ and } B)}{P(B)}
\]


Example 1 (die roll): Consider the trial of rolling a fair six-sided die once.
Let \(A\) be the event “the roll is a 3” and let \(B\) be the event “the roll is odd.”

List the outcomes in \(A\), in \(B\), and in \(A \text{ and } B\).
Compute \(P(A)\), \(P(B)\), and \(P(A \text{ and } B)\).
Find \(P(A \mid B)\): the probability of getting a 3 given the roll resulted in an odd number.
Find \(P(B \mid A)\): the probability of getting an odd number given the roll resulted in a 3.







NoteWorked solution — die Example 1




\(A=\{3\}\), \(B=\{1,3,5\}\), \(A\cap B=\{3\}\).
\(P(A)=1/6\), \(P(B)=3/6=1/2\), \(P(A\text{ and }B)=1/6\).
\(P(A|B)=(1/6)/(1/2)=1/3\).
\(P(B|A)=1\) (if the roll is 3, it is odd for sure).



Practice Problem 1: A jar contains 10 candies: 6 are red and 4 are blue. Two candies are selected without replacement.
Let \(A\) be the event “the first candy is red” and \(B\) be the event “the second candy is red.”

Find \(P(A)\).
Find \(P(B \mid A)\).
Use the multiplication rule (below) to find \(P(A \text{ and } B)\).







NoteWorked solution — candy jar




\(P(A)=6/10\). b. \(P(B|A)=5/9\). c. \(P(A\text{ and }B)=(6/10)(5/9)=1/3\).










ImportantDefinition: Multiplication rule



For any two events \(A\) and \(B\) with \(P(B) > 0\),
\[
P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A \mid B)\,P(B)
\]
Equivalently (if \(P(A) > 0\)),
\[
P(A \text{ and } B) = P(B \mid A)\,P(A)
\]
Example 2 (two cards, no replacement): A card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck, then a second card is drawn without replacement.
Find the probability the first card is an Ace and the second card is a King.






NoteWorked solution — Ace then King



\(P = (4/52)(4/51) = 16/2652 = 4/663\).



Events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent if knowing that one event occurred does not change the probability of the other.
Equivalent ways to check independence:

\(P(A \mid B) = P(A)\) (when \(P(B) > 0\))
\(P(B \mid A) = P(B)\) (when \(P(A) > 0\))
\(P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A)\,P(B)\)

Example 3 (king vs spade): Suppose a card is randomly dealt from a standard 52-card deck.
Is the event “the card is a king” independent of the event “the card is a spade”?

Multiplication Rule for Two Independent Events
If \(A\) and \(B\) are independent, then
\[
P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A)\,P(B)
\]


Example 4 (two coin tosses): Suppose a fair coin is tossed twice.
Find the probability of getting “heads” on the first toss and “tails” on the second toss.
Practice Problem 2: Suppose a fair six-sided die is rolled twice.
Let \(A\) be the event “the first roll is even” and let \(B\) be the event “the second roll is 6.”

Are \(A\) and \(B\) independent? (Explain briefly.)
Compute \(P(A \text{ and } B)\).







NoteWorked solution — two die rolls




Yes, independent (separate rolls).
\(P(A\text{ and }B)=P(A)P(B)=(3/6)(1/6)=1/12\).









TipCheck yourself — Conditional probability and independence




In words, what does \(P(A \mid B)\) mean?
Write the formula for \(P(A \mid B)\) when \(P(B) > 0\).
State the multiplication rule for \(P(A \text{ and } B)\).
Give two equivalent ways to check that \(A\) and \(B\) are independent.
Fair die: find \(P(\text{roll is 2} \mid \text{roll is even})\).
Two fair coin tosses: find \(P(\text{H on first and T on second})\).





Click to reveal answers


The probability that \(A\) occurs given that \(B\) has already occurred.
\(P(A \mid B) = P(A \text{ and } B) / P(B)\).
\(P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A \mid B)\,P(B)\) (equivalently \(P(B \mid A)\,P(A)\) when \(P(A)>0\)).
\(P(A \mid B) = P(A)\), or \(P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A)\,P(B)\).
Given even \(\{2,4,6\}\), one of three is 2: \(P = 1/3\).
\(P = (1/2)(1/2) = 1/4\) (independent trials).






Learning Outcomes:

Distinguish between situations where order matters (permutations) and where order does not matter (combinations).
Use the formulas for \(_nP_r\) and \(_nC_r\) to solve counting problems.





Problem (a). Find the number of ways to distribute 3 distinct flavors of ice cream to 3 distinct bowls.






NoteWorked solution — ice cream (a)



\(3! = 6\) ways (order matters).



Problem (b). Find the number of ways to choose 2 distinct flavors of ice cream from 26 flavors to create an ice cream cone with one scoop on the top and one scoop on the bottom.






NoteWorked solution — ice cream (b)



\(_{26}P_2 = 26 \times 25 = 650\) (order matters).



Problem (c). Find the number of ways to choose 2 distinct flavors of ice cream from 26 flavors to create a dish with two scoops of ice cream, where the order of the scoops doesn’t matter.






NoteWorked solution — ice cream (c)



\(_{26}C_2 = 26 \times 25 / 2 = 325\).












ImportantDefinitions: Permutation and combination




Permutation: An arrangement of objects where order matters. (Chocolate on top, vanilla on bottom \(\neq\) vanilla on top, chocolate on bottom.)
Combination: A selection of objects where order does not matter. (Chocolate + vanilla in a dish = vanilla + chocolate.)










ImportantDefinition: Factorial



The factorial of a nonnegative integer \(n\), written \(n!\), is the product of all positive integers from \(n\) down to 1:
\[
n! = n \times (n-1) \times (n-2) \times \cdots \times 2 \times 1
\]
Convention: \(0! = 1\). (This is defined so that our permutation and combination formulas work correctly when \(r = n\) or \(r = 0\).)
Examples:

\(3! = 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 6\)
\(5! = 5 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 120\)
\(1! = 1\)










ImportantFormulas: Permutations and combinations



Permutations \(_nP_r\) (or \(P(n,r)\)): The number of ways to arrange \(r\) objects chosen from \(n\) distinct objects, where order matters.
\[
_nP_r = \frac{n!}{(n-r)!} = n(n-1)(n-2)\cdots(n-r+1)
\]
Combinations \(_nC_r\) (or \(\binom{n}{r}\) or \(C(n,r)\)): The number of ways to choose \(r\) objects from \(n\) distinct objects, where order does not matter.
\[
_nC_r = \binom{n}{r} = \frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!} = \frac{_nP_r}{r!}
\]
Relationship: \(_nC_r = \dfrac{_nP_r}{r!}\) — we divide by \(r!\) because each combination of \(r\) objects can be arranged in \(r!\) different orders, and we want to count them once.






Suppose we have 5 letters: A, B, C, D, E. We want to choose 3 of them.
Part 1 (order matters): How many ways can we choose 3 letters if the order of our choice matters? (e.g., for a 3-letter code)?






NoteWorked solution — letters, order matters



\(_{5}P_3 = 5 \times 4 \times 3 = 60\).



Part 2 (order doesn’t matter): How many ways can we choose 3 letters if the order of our choice does not matter (e.g., for a committee of 3)?






NoteWorked solution — letters, committee



\(_{5}C_3 = 10\).






Rule of thumb: Ask yourself: “If I swap two of the chosen items, do I get a different outcome?” If yes → permutation. If no → combination.






TipCheck yourself — Counting and combinations




What is the difference between a permutation and a combination?
Compute \(4!\) and state the value of \(0!\).
Compute \(_5C_2\) and \(_5P_2\).
How many ways to choose 3 people from 7 for a committee (order does not matter)?
Why does \(_nC_r = _nP_r / r!\)?





Click to reveal answers


Permutation: order matters. Combination: order does not matter (a selection).
\(4! = 24\); \(0! = 1\) by convention.
\(_5C_2 = 10\); \(_5P_2 = 20\).
\(\binom{7}{3} = 35\).
Each combination of \(r\) objects can be arranged in \(r!\) orders; dividing counts each selection once.






Learning Outcomes:

Define random variable and its probability distribution function (pdf) (for discrete random variables).
Define a binomial random variable and a binomial random process.
Match the notation (\(n\), \(x\), \(p\)) and four conditions for a binomial process with the process of tossing a coin.
Express probabilities for binomial random variables via the binomial pdf formula.





A random variable is defined as…














ImportantDefinition: Probability distribution function (pdf)



For a discrete random variable \(X\), the probability distribution function (or probability mass function) gives the probability that \(X\) takes each possible value. We write \(f(x) = P(X = x)\) for each possible value \(x\).






Example 1. A coin is tossed \(n = 1\) time; \(p\) = probability of heads. Find an expression for \(f(x) = P(X = x)\) for \(x = 0\) and \(x = 1\).






NoteWorked solution — \(n=1\)



\(f(0)=1-p\), \(f(1)=p\).



Example 2. A coin is tossed \(n = 2\) times; \(p\) = probability of heads. Find an expression for \(f(x)\) for \(x = 0, 1, 2\).






NoteWorked solution — \(n=2\)



\(f(0)=(1-p)^2\), \(f(1)=2p(1-p)\), \(f(2)=p^2\).



Example 3. A coin is tossed \(n = 3\) times; \(p\) = probability of heads. Find an expression for \(f(x)\) for \(x = 0, 1, 2, 3\).






NoteWorked solution — \(n=3\)



\(f(0)=(1-p)^3\), \(f(1)=3p(1-p)^2\), \(f(2)=3p^2(1-p)\), \(f(3)=p^3\).



Example 4. A coin is tossed \(n = 4\) times; \(p\) = probability of heads. Find an expression for \(f(x)\) for \(x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4\).






NoteWorked solution — \(n=4\)



Coefficients 1, 4, 6, 4, 1: \(f(x)=\binom{4}{x}p^x(1-p)^{4-x}\).



General case. A coin is tossed \(n\) times; \(p\) = probability of heads. Find an expression for \(f(x) = P(X = x)\) for \(x = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, n\).



A binomial random variable \(X\) counts the number of “successes” in a binomial random process.






ImportantDefinition: Four BRP conditions



Four conditions for a binomial random process:

Fixed number of trials \(n\) (e.g., \(n\) coin tosses).
Two outcomes on each trial: “success” or “failure” (e.g., heads vs tails).
Independent trials — the outcome of one trial does not affect the others.
Constant probability \(p\) of success on each trial (e.g., same \(p\) for every toss).

Notation: \(n\) = number of trials, \(p\) = probability of success on one trial, \(X\) = number of successes, and \(x\) = a specific value of \(X\) (0, 1, 2, …, \(n\)).












ImportantDefinition: Binomial pmf



If \(X\) is binomial with \(n\) trials and success probability \(p\), then for \(x = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, n\),
\[ P(X = x) = f(x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x} = _nC_x\, p^x (1-p)^{n-x} \]
where \(\binom{n}{x} = _nC_x = \dfrac{n!}{x!(n-x)!}\) is the number of ways to choose \(x\) successes out of \(n\) trials.


————————————————————————##






TipCheck yourself — Random variables and the binomial process




What is a random variable?
For discrete \(X\), what does the pmf \(f(x) = P(X = x)\) mean?
List the four BRP conditions.
In words, what do \(n\), \(p\), \(X\), and \(x\) mean in a binomial setting?





Click to reveal answers


A rule that assigns a number to each outcome in a sample space (written with capitals such as \(X\)).
\(f(x)\) is the probability that the random variable \(X\) equals the specific value \(x\).

Binary outcome each trial. (b) Fixed \(n\). (c) Fixed \(p\) each trial. (d) Independent trials.

\(n\) = number of trials; \(p\) = success probability on one trial; \(X\) = random count of successes; \(x\) = a specific possible value of \(X\).













ImportantDefinitions and formula summary (binomial)



Notation:

\(n\) = number of trials
\(p\) = probability of “success” on a single trial
\(x\) = observed number of successes in \(n\) trials
\(X\) = random variable that counts the number of successes in \(n\) trials

Factorial: \(n! = n(n-1)(n-2)\cdots(3)(2)(1)\)
Counting:

\(_nC_x = \binom{n}{x} = \dfrac{n!}{x!(n-x)!}\)
\(_nP_x = \dfrac{n!}{(n-x)!}\)

Four conditions for a binomial random process (BRP):

Each trial results in either “success” or “failure”.
Outcomes between trials are independent.
The probability of success \(p\) is the same on every trial.
A fixed number of trials \(n\) are observed.

Binomial random variable: \(X\) = number of successes in \(n\) trials when data are collected from a BRP.
Probability distribution function (pdf) for a binomial random variable \(X\):
\[
f(x) = P(X = x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x} = _nC_x\, p^x (1-p)^{n-x}
\]
Cumulative probability: \(P(X \leq x) = f(0) + f(1) + f(2) + \cdots + f(x)\)
Note: \(P(X > x) = 1 - P(X \leq x) = f(x+1) + f(x+2) + \cdots + f(n)\)
Mean of \(X\): \(\mu = np\)
Standard deviation of \(X\): \(\sigma = \sqrt{np(1-p)}\)








Which of the following situations is an example of data being collected from a binomial random process? Be prepared to justify your answer by discussing the validity of each of the four conditions.

Rolling a six-sided die 15 times and counting the number of times a “3” was obtained.
Picking 10 gummy vitamins from a bottle that contains 100 vitamins of various animal shapes. Count the number of lions, tigers, and bears in the set of 10.
Drawing cards one at a time from a deck of 52, counting the number of kings drawn. After each card is drawn, it is replaced in the deck, the deck is shuffled, and another card is drawn.
Drawing cards one at a time from a deck of 52, counting the number of kings drawn. After each card is drawn, it is not replaced in the deck.
Giving a class activity to 20 students and counting the number of these students who ask a question about it during class.







NoteWorked solution — which is binomial?



(c) is binomial (fixed \(n\), binary king/not, replacement keeps \(p\) constant, independent draws). (a) can be binomial if success = “3”. (b) is not (more than two categories). (d) is not (\(p\) changes). (e) is not a standard BRP (trials not identical random process).






For each situation below, identify \(n\), \(p\), and the appropriate value to compare to \(X\), then write an expression for the probability using the pdf of a binomial random variable.

Problem 2. Suppose Bob flips a fair coin 4 times. What is the probability he gets exactly 2 heads?






NoteWorked solution — exactly 2 heads



\(n=4\), \(p=0.5\), \(P(X=2)=\binom{4}{2}(0.5)^4=6/16=3/8\).



Problem 3. Suppose Neal has an unfair coin: it has an 80% chance of landing “heads”. What is the probability that he gets exactly 2 heads if he tosses the coin 4 times?






NoteWorked solution — unfair coin



\(P(X=2)=\binom{4}{2}(0.8)^2(0.2)^2=6(0.64)(0.04)=0.1536\).



Problem 4. Suppose that in a week of 7 days, there is a 65% chance of rain on any single day. What is the probability of it raining on at least 2 of the 7 days? On at most 2 of the 7 days?






NoteWorked solution — rain days



\(n=7\), \(p=0.65\). At least 2: \(P(X\ge 2)=1-P(X\le 1)\). At most 2: \(P(X\le 2)=f(0)+f(1)+f(2)\) (or pbinom(2,7,0.65)).



Problem 5. Suppose customers at a coffee shop can order either iced or hot coffee. Sharon observes 6 customers ordering one day: of these, only 2 order iced coffee. If 10% of all customers order iced coffee, what is the probability of observing 2 or more iced orders (under this model)?






NoteWorked solution — iced coffee



\(n=6\), \(p=0.10\). \(P(X\ge 2)=1-P(X\le 1)\) (or 1-pbinom(1,6,0.10)).



Problem 6. Compute the mean and standard deviation of the random variable \(X\) that is the number of “heads” in 25 tosses of a fair coin.






NoteWorked solution — mean and SD



\(\mu=np=25(0.5)=12.5\). \(\sigma=\sqrt{np(1-p)}=\sqrt{25(0.5)(0.5)}=2.5\).








TipCheck yourself — Binomial pmf




Write the binomial pmf \(P(X = x)\).
A fair coin is flipped 12 times. Identify \(n\), \(p\), and what \(x\) represents.
20% of seeds fail to germinate; you plant 8 seeds. Identify \(n\) and \(p\) if \(X\) = number that fail.
Write \(\binom{n}{x}\) in factorial form.





Click to reveal answers


\(P(X=x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x}\) for \(x = 0, 1, \ldots, n\).
\(n = 12\) trials; \(p = 0.5\); \(x\) is a possible number of heads (0 through 12).
\(n = 8\), \(p = 0.20\).
\(\binom{n}{x} = n! / [x!(n-x)!]\).

title: Module 1 — Read 1
text:
NoteExample in-class data (illustrative)



Suppose three students record: Rosanna 7 heads in 10 tosses (\(\hat{p}=0.7\)); You 4 heads in 10 (\(\hat{p}=0.4\)); Neighbor 6 heads in 12 (\(\hat{p}=0.5\)). Counts and proportions differ because \(n\) and randomness differ.


Let’s toss a coin a few times in class, keeping track of the tosses that land “heads.”



Count of heads (\(x\)): 7
Total tosses (\(n\)): 10
Proportion (\(\hat{p}\)): 0.7
Percentage: 70%





Count of heads (\(x\)): 4
Total tosses (\(n\)): 10
Proportion (\(\hat{p}\)): 0.4
Percentage: 40%





Count of heads (\(x\)): 6
Total tosses (\(n\)): 12
Proportion (\(\hat{p}\)): 0.5
Percentage: 50%

What’s the highest count of heads? 7 (Rosanna)
Most tosses? 12 (neighbor)
Highest proportion of heads? 0.7 (Rosanna)
Highest percentage of heads? 70% (Rosanna)
Comments:
If we care about comparing coins (with the same number of tosses), then \(\hat{p}\) (proportion) is the best summary.
If we care about getting lots of “heads” then \(x\) (count) is the best summary.
The summary of total tosses (\(n\)) tells us how much data we collected / how precise the proportion can be.
Question: Rosanna keeps tossing her coin forever. What would we expect?

Data (what happened): varies from sample to sample (e.g. \(\hat{p}\) bounces around)
Theory (long run): approaches 0.5 for a fair coin

Fill in each definition in your own words:

Sample space:


Outcome:

ImportantNotation: Data vs theory




We’ll use two colors: one for observed data and another for theoretical quantities.
Async note: In class we color-code theoretical vs observed quantities. On your own, pick two highlighters and use them consistently for \(P(\text{event})\) vs \(\hat{p}\).

\(x\) = count of “successes” in \(n\) observed trials
\(n\) = number of observed trials
\(\hat{p} = x/n\) = observed proportion of successes in our trials
Percentage of observed trials that were a success \(= 100 \cdot \hat{p}\)
\(P(\text{event})\) = probability of an event

The notation for probability, \(P(\text{event})\), is in the same format as notation for functions in high school algebra:

\(=\) reads as “is” (or “equals”)
\(()\) reads as “of” — the event inside the parentheses (not multiplication!)

\(Y = f(x)\) reads as “\(y\) is the value of the function whose name is \(f\) when \(x\) is put in.”
\(Y = P(A)\) reads as “\(y\) is the value of probability when the event under consideration is \(A\).”

title: Module 1 — Read 1
text:
A die is rolled 30 times and shows “1” exactly 10 times. Fill in:

\(x = 10\)
\(n = 30\)
\(\hat{p} = 10/30 \approx 0.333\)
Percentage \(\approx 33.3\%\)
Theoretical \(P(\text{"1"}) = 1/6\)








ImportantRules for probabilities (axioms)



All probabilities must satisfy:

\(0 \le P(A) \le 1\) for any event \(A\)
Total probability across all possible outcomes \(= 1\)
If \(A\) and \(B\) are two events with no overlap, then \(P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B)\)






Coin: \(P(\text{Heads}) + P(\text{Tails}) =\) 1
Die: \(P(\text{"1"}) + P(\text{"2"}) + \cdots + P(\text{"6"}) =\) 1
Die: \(P(\text{"1"}) + P(\text{"2"}) =\) \(1/3\)
\(P(A) = 70\) is invalid (probabilities must be between 0 and 1)
\(-0.5 = P(B)\) is invalid (cannot be negative)
\(P(D) = 0.7\) is valid








ImportantDefinition: Probability



\(P(\text{Event})\) is the proportion of times the event occurs out of the number of trials as the trial is repeated infinitely many times.
Probability is tied to:

A specific random process (repeating a trial with uncertain outcome infinitely many times)
Long-run relative frequency (a.k.a. “proportion”) of an event occurring

Suppose Allen, Beth and Cal are in an elevator, each holding a green lunchbox when an earthquake occurs. In the resulting chaos, their lunch boxes are dropped and shuffled around. Assuming they each pick up one lunch box, find the probability that they each pick up their own lunch box.

Two outcomes: (5,6) and (6,5). \(P = 2/36 = 1/18\).

title: Module 1 — Read 1
text:
Learning Outcomes:

State the Addition Rule for any two events
Use the addition rule to compute the probability of events A or B, being aware of special cases.








ImportantDefinition: Addition rule



For any two events \(A\) and \(B\),
\[P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B)\]
Equivalently, \(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\).


Visualizing the Addition Rule with a Venn Diagram






NoteVenn diagram idea



Draw overlapping circles for \(A\) and \(B\). \(P(A\text{ or }B)\) covers both circles but subtract the overlap \(P(A\text{ and }B)\) so it is not counted twice.


Example: Suppose a class consists of 20 students.  Of these students, 12 have backpacks and 3 have hats.  There is only 1 student with both a backpack and a hat. 
Suppose one student is randomly selected from the 20.  What is the probability this student will either have a backpack OR have a hat?






NoteWorked solution — backpacks and hats (20 students)



\(P(\text{backpack or hat}) = 12/20 + 3/20 - 1/20 = 14/20 = 0.7\).


Practice Problem: Suppose a class consists of 30 students.  Of these students, 8 like to go sky diving and 20 like to go surfing.  There are 7 students that like both sky diving and surfing.
Suppose one student is randomly selected from the 30.  What is the probability this student will like sky diving OR surfing






NoteWorked solution — sky diving or surfing



\(P = 8/30 + 20/30 - 7/30 = 21/30 = 0.7\).



Special Cases of the Addition Rule






ImportantDefinition: Complement rule



For any event \(A\),
\[P(\text{not } A) = P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)\]








ImportantDefinition: Disjoint (non-overlapping) events



If \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint (non-overlapping), then \(P(A \text{ and } B) = 0\) and
\[P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B)\]


Example: Suppose the probability of it snowing at least once this November is 0.83.  what is the probability that it will not snow at all this November?






NoteWorked solution — complement



\(P(\text{no snow}) = 1 - 0.83 = 0.17\).


Example: Suppose that a brand of gummy vitamins come in three animal shapes: Lions, tigers or bears .  The company creates the gummies as follows: 30% of the shapes are bears, 30% are tigers and 40% are lions. 
What is the probability that a randomly selected gummy will be either a bear or a tiger?






NoteWorked solution — disjoint gummies



Bear and tiger are disjoint: \(P = 0.30 + 0.30 = 0.60\).


Practice Problem: Suppose a card is drawn from a standard 52 card deck.  What is the probability the card is…

A “face” card (king, queen or jack)?
An Ace?
Not an Ace?







NoteWorked solution — card from deck




Face cards: \(12/52 = 3/13\). b. Ace: \(4/52 = 1/13\). c. Not an Ace: \(48/52 = 12/13\).









TipCheck yourself — Addition rule




State the addition rule for any events \(A\) and \(B\).
State the complement rule for event \(A\).
If \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint, what is \(P(A \text{ and } B)\)? Write the simplified addition rule.
Class: 40 with backpacks, 10 with hats, 5 with both (out of 65). Find \(P(\text{backpack or hat})\).
If \(P(\text{rains at least once in July}) = 0.91\), find \(P(\text{no rain in July})\).





Click to reveal answers


\(P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B)\).
\(P(A^c) = P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A)\).
\(P(A \text{ and } B) = 0\) and \(P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B)\).
\(P(A)=40/65\), \(P(B)=10/65\), \(P(A\text{ and }B)=5/65\). \(P(A\text{ or }B)=45/65 \approx 0.69\).
